title: Quicksort: partition, recursion, and why the worst case is n²
summary: Trace Lomuto partition (pivot, i, j, the final swap, the return value); run quicksort's recursion on an array; write its recurrence and explain the Θ(n²) worst case, the Θ(n log n) best and average case, and how real libraries avoid the worst case.
sourceNote: Lecture 9 'Quicksort' (Sep 21) slides, HW 9, CLRS ch. 7. Builds on merge sort (Lecture 5) and recurrences (Lectures 6 and 7). Real-world notes are general industry practice.

sections.heading: The big picture: sort in place by picking a pivot

blocks.md: Merge sort is always n log n but needs a second array. Heap sort needs no extra array but is fiddly and not very cache-friendly. **Quicksort** sorts inside the one array and, on typical data, is the fastest of the three. Its one weakness is a bad pivot, and this chapter shows exactly when that happens and how real code avoids it.

sections.heading: The idea: line a class up by height

blocks.md: **Poon's analogy: sorting by height** Pick one student as the **pivot**. Everyone shorter moves to their left, everyone taller to their right. The pivot is now standing exactly where they would be in a fully sorted line, even though the two groups are still messy. Now do the same thing inside each group. When every group is size 0 or 1, the whole line is sorted.

blocks.body: The one element chosen to split the array. After partitioning, smaller-or-equal elements are to its left, larger to its right, and **the pivot is in its final sorted position**. In this lecture the pivot is always the **last** element of the part being sorted (this is called **Lomuto** quicksort).

blocks.md: **Why pick one item and not sort everything at once?** Because placing ONE item correctly is cheap (one pass, O(n)) and it splits the problem in two independent halves that never need to be combined. Do that again inside each half, and the whole thing sorts itself.
blocks.label: why

sections.heading: partition: the one step that does all the work

blocks.body: Works only on `a[low..high]`. Picks `pivot = a[high]`, moves every element ≤ pivot to the left part, puts the pivot right after them, and **returns the pivot's new index**.

frames.caption: partition(a, 0, 4): the pivot is the LAST item, 5. i = -1 (the '≤ pivot' zone is empty). j will scout from 0 to 3.
j = 0: 9 > 5. Leave it: it joins the amber '> 5' zone. Only j moves on.
j = 1: 3 ≤ 5. It belongs in the green zone: i++ → 0, then swap a[0] and a[1].
The green '≤ 5' zone grew to a[0..0].
j = 2: 1 ≤ 5. It belongs in the green zone: i++ → 1, then swap a[1] and a[2].
The green '≤ 5' zone grew to a[0..1].
j = 3: 7 > 5. Leave it: it joins the amber '> 5' zone. Only j moves on.
The scout is done. Last move: swap the pivot into a[i + 1] = a[2], right after the green zone.
5 is now at index 2, its FINAL sorted position: everything left is ≤ 5, everything right is > 5. Return 2.

blocks.md: Watch the colors: **green** is 'known to be ≤ pivot', **amber** is 'known to be > pivot', white is 'not checked yet'. **j is the scout** walking right; **i is the boundary** of the green zone. A small item gets swapped into the green zone; a big one is simply walked past.

blocks.title: The pseudocode (Lecture 9)
blocks.body:
partition(a, low, high):
    pivot = a[high]
    i = low - 1              // zone of '≤ pivot' is empty
    for j = low to high - 1  // j scouts, skips pivot
        if a[j] <= pivot
            i++              // grow the zone
            swap a[i] with a[j]  // pull it in
    swap a[i+1] with a[high] // pivot after zone
    return i + 1

blocks.title: Your turn from the slides: partition(a, 2, 7) on [19, 9, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 3, 4, 6]

frames.caption: partition(a, 2, 7): the pivot is the LAST item, 3. i = 1 (the '≤ pivot' zone is empty). j will scout from 2 to 6.
j = 2: 5 > 3. Leave it: it joins the amber '> 3' zone. Only j moves on.
j = 3: 1 ≤ 3. It belongs in the green zone: i++ → 2, then swap a[2] and a[3].
The green '≤ 3' zone grew to a[2..2].
j = 4: 8 > 3. Leave it: it joins the amber '> 3' zone. Only j moves on.
j = 5: 7 > 3. Leave it: it joins the amber '> 3' zone. Only j moves on.
j = 6: 2 ≤ 3. It belongs in the green zone: i++ → 3, then swap a[3] and a[6].
The green '≤ 3' zone grew to a[2..3].
The scout is done. Last move: swap the pivot into a[i + 1] = a[4], right after the green zone.
3 is now at index 4, its FINAL sorted position: everything left is ≤ 3, everything right is > 3. Return 4.

blocks.md: **The invariant that makes partition correct:** at every moment, a[low..i] ≤ pivot, a[i+1..j−1] > pivot, a[j..high−1] unchecked, a[high] = pivot. Each step keeps it true; when j reaches high, one swap puts the pivot between the two zones.
blocks.label: think

blocks.caption: Pick *quicksort* and press Next to watch every partition step. Then type your own array. Try an already sorted one like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and count the comparisons.

blocks.md: **Runtime of partition** The loop runs once for each element from `low` to `high − 1`, doing constant work each time. So partition on n elements is **Θ(n)**.

blocks.body: Returning i instead of i + 1. After the loop, i points at the last small element; the pivot goes one to the right of it, at i + 1, and that is what partition returns.

Counting indexes from `low` instead of from 0. partition returns an index into the **whole** array. On the slide's 'Your turn' (a = [19, 9, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 3, 4, 6], low = 2, high = 7), the pivot is a[7] = 3 and it lands at **index 4** of the whole array. The slide's answer says 'index 3' because its picture starts at a[1]; when you write your own answer, count from a[0].

blocks.title: Your turn: write partition
blocks.task: Write Lomuto `partition(a, low, high)` in Python: pivot = a[high], i = low − 1, scout j from low to high − 1, final swap, return i + 1.
blocks.starter:
def partition(a, low, high):
    pivot = a[high]
    i = low - 1
    # for j in range(low, high): if a[j] <= pivot: i += 1 and swap a[i], a[j]
    # then swap a[i + 1] with a[high] and return i + 1
    return -1

a = [9, 3, 1, 7, 5]
p = partition(a, 0, 4)
print(a, "pivot landed at", p)     # expect [3, 1, 5, 7, 9] 2
blocks.check:
a = [9, 3, 1, 7, 5]
p = partition(a, 0, 4)
assert (a, p) == ([3, 1, 5, 7, 9], 2), f"partition([9, 3, 1, 7, 5], 0, 4) should leave [3, 1, 5, 7, 9] and return 2. Got {a}, {p}."
b = [19, 9, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 3, 4, 6]
p = partition(b, 2, 7)
assert p == 4 and b == [19, 9, 1, 2, 3, 7, 5, 8, 4, 6], f"partition(b, 2, 7) should return 4 (an index into the WHOLE array) and leave a[0..1] and a[8..9] untouched. Got {b}, {p}."
c = [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert partition(c, 0, 3) == 3, "On sorted input the pivot (the max) stays at the end: return 3."
blocks.solution:
def partition(a, low, high):
    pivot = a[high]
    i = low - 1
    for j in range(low, high):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i + 1], a[high] = a[high], a[i + 1]
    return i + 1

a = [9, 3, 1, 7, 5]
p = partition(a, 0, 4)
print(a, "pivot landed at", p)
hints: `for j in range(low, high):` stops BEFORE high, the pivot.
Inside: `if a[j] <= pivot: i += 1; a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]`.
After the loop: `a[i + 1], a[high] = a[high], a[i + 1]` and `return i + 1`.
blocks.success: Ten lines, and the heart of the fastest general-purpose sort. It's also one of the most-asked interview snippets.

blocks.prompt: partition([4, 8, 2, 6, 5], 0, 4): what is the array afterwards, and what is returned?
blocks.answer: Pivot 5. j=0: 4 ≤ 5, i=0 (swap with itself). j=1: 8 skip. j=2: 2 ≤ 5, i=1, swap → [4, 2, 8, 6, 5]. j=3: 6 skip. Final swap a[2] ↔ a[4] → [4, 2, 5, 6, 8]. Return 2.

sections.heading: quicksort: partition, then recurse on both sides

blocks.title: The pseudocode
blocks.body:
quicksort(a, low, high):
    if low < high                  // 2+ elements
        p = partition(a, low, high) // p is final
        quicksort(a, low, p - 1)    // left side
        quicksort(a, p + 1, high)   // right side

First call: quicksort(a, 0, n - 1)

frames.caption: quicksort(a, 0, 7) on [2, 8, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]. Each call partitions its range, which puts ONE pivot in its final spot, then recurses on the two sides.
quicksort(0, 7): work only on a[0..7]. Pivot = a[7] = 4.
After partition: 4 lands at index 3, final. Left of it ≤ 4, right of it > 4. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(0, 2): work only on a[0..2]. Pivot = a[2] = 3.
After partition: 3 lands at index 2, final. Left of it ≤ 3, right of it > 3. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(0, 1): work only on a[0..1]. Pivot = a[1] = 1.
After partition: 1 lands at index 0, final. Left of it ≤ 1, right of it > 1. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(1, 1): one item is already sorted (base case). a[1] = 2 is final.
quicksort(4, 7): work only on a[4..7]. Pivot = a[7] = 8.
After partition: 8 lands at index 7, final. Left of it ≤ 8, right of it > 8. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(4, 6): work only on a[4..6]. Pivot = a[6] = 6.
After partition: 6 lands at index 5, final. Left of it ≤ 6, right of it > 6. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(4, 4): one item is already sorted (base case). a[4] = 5 is final.
quicksort(6, 6): one item is already sorted (base case). a[6] = 7 is final.
Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], in place. No merge step was ever needed: once both sides of every pivot are sorted, everything is.

blocks.md: Notice what is **not** there: no merge step. Once the pivot is in place and both sides are sorted, the whole range is sorted, because every left item ≤ pivot < every right item. And the pivot is **left out** of both recursive calls (p − 1 and p + 1): it's already done.
That table is the one idea to remember: merge sort does its work on the way **up** (merging), quicksort does its work on the way **down** (partitioning).

blocks.prompt: In quicksort(a, low, high), why is the base case `low < high` and not `low <= high`?
blocks.answer: When low = high there is one element, and one element is already sorted. When low > high the range is empty. Both mean: nothing to do.

sections.heading: How fast? It depends on the pivot

blocks.title: The recurrence
blocks.body:
Let q = size of the left side after partition.
The right side has n − q − 1 (the pivot is in neither).

T(n) = T(q) + T(n − q − 1) + Θ(n)
                              └ partition

blocks.md: Unlike merge sort, **q is not fixed**. It depends on where the pivot lands, which depends on the data. So there is no single recurrence; there is a best one and a worst one.

cards.title: Good pivots
lines: log n levels, n work per level

cards.title: Bad pivots
lines: n levels, each one item shorter

data.note: Each bar is one level of the recursion: how many pieces (good) or how big the one piece is (bad). Lomuto on **already sorted** input always picks the max as pivot, so it's always the bad shape.

blocks.caption: The pivot decides the shape of the recursion, and the shape decides the running time.

blocks.title: Worst case: the input is already sorted
blocks.body:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The pivot (last) is always the biggest.
Left side gets n − 1 elements, right side gets 0.

T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(0) + Θ(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n)
     = n + (n − 1) + … + 2 + 1
     = n(n + 1)/2 = Θ(n²)

blocks.title: The worst case: quicksort on already sorted [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

frames.caption: quicksort(a, 0, 4) on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Each call partitions its range, which puts ONE pivot in its final spot, then recurses on the two sides.
quicksort(0, 4): work only on a[0..4]. Pivot = a[4] = 5.
After partition: 5 lands at index 4, final. Left of it ≤ 5, right of it > 5. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(0, 3): work only on a[0..3]. Pivot = a[3] = 4.
After partition: 4 lands at index 3, final. Left of it ≤ 4, right of it > 4. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(0, 2): work only on a[0..2]. Pivot = a[2] = 3.
After partition: 3 lands at index 2, final. Left of it ≤ 3, right of it > 3. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(0, 1): work only on a[0..1]. Pivot = a[1] = 2.
After partition: 2 lands at index 1, final. Left of it ≤ 2, right of it > 2. Now recurse on each side.
quicksort(0, 0): one item is already sorted (base case). a[0] = 1 is final.
Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], in place. No merge step was ever needed: once both sides of every pivot are sorted, everything is.

blocks.title: Best case: the pivot lands in the middle every time
blocks.body:
Both sides get about n/2.

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)

That is exactly merge sort's recurrence. Master method case 2 → Θ(n log n).

blocks.md: **Average case** On random input the splits are uneven but not terrible, and quicksort is still **Θ(n log n)**. Even a lopsided 9-to-1 split at every level gives Θ(n log n): the tree is deeper (log base 10/9 instead of 2) but still logarithmic, and each level still costs Θ(n). CLRS 7.4 has the proof.

blocks.title: The three n log n sorts (Lecture 9 slide 31)
blocks.slide: Quicksort vs merge sort vs heap sort

blocks.body: Saying quicksort's worst case is n log n, or that it happens on random input. The worst case is Θ(n²), and for Lomuto it happens on **already sorted** (or reverse sorted) input, the input you would think is easiest.

blocks.prompt: Why does quicksort use O(log n) extra space if it sorts in place?
blocks.answer: The recursion itself: each pending call sits on the call stack. With balanced splits the recursion is about log n deep. (In the worst case it is n deep.)

sections.heading: How real code avoids the worst case

blocks.md: Nobody ships the version from class as-is: one sorted input and it crawls. Real implementations change **how the pivot is chosen** or **how partition works**.

rows: pick a random index, swap it to the end, then partition as usual
sorted input no longer means bad pivots; the n² case becomes astronomically unlikely
pivot = median of first, middle, last
a sorted array now gets a perfect middle pivot
two markers start at both ends and walk toward each other, swapping out-of-place pairs
fewer swaps than Lomuto on average
blocks.title: Three fixes (Lecture 9 slide 33)

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet it.** Java's `Arrays.sort` on primitive arrays is a dual-pivot quicksort. C++'s `std::sort` is **introsort**: quicksort that switches to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep (so the worst case is n log n) and to insertion sort on tiny pieces, the same trick as Project 1's hybrid. Database engines use quicksort-style partitioning for in-memory sorts, and 'quickselect' (partition, then recurse on ONE side) finds a median or the top-k in O(n) on average.
blocks.label: world

blocks.md: **Use quicksort** (your library's sort) for general in-memory sorting where average speed matters most. **Use merge sort / Timsort** when you need stability or a guaranteed n log n on adversarial input. **Use heap sort** when memory is tight and you need a guarantee. **Use partition alone** (quickselect) when you only need the k-th smallest, not a full sort.
blocks.label: when

blocks.title: See it: sorted input vs random input
blocks.task: This counts quicksort's comparisons on a random list and on an already sorted list of the same size, with a last-element pivot and with a random pivot. Run it and compare the last two columns.
blocks.starter:
import random, sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

def quicksort(a, lo, hi, pick, count):
    if lo < hi:
        k = pick(lo, hi)
        a[k], a[hi] = a[hi], a[k]           # move the chosen pivot to the end
        pivot, i = a[hi], lo - 1
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            count[0] += 1
            if a[j] <= pivot:
                i += 1
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
        a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]
        quicksort(a, lo, i, pick, count)
        quicksort(a, i + 2, hi, pick, count)

last = lambda lo, hi: hi
rand = lambda lo, hi: random.randint(lo, hi)

for n in [200, 800, 1600]:
    row = []
    for data in (random.sample(range(n), n), list(range(n))):
        for pick in (last, rand):
            c = [0]
            quicksort(list(data), 0, n - 1, pick, c)
            row.append(c[0])
    print(f"n = {n:5}: random+last {row[0]:8,}  random+rand {row[1]:8,}  SORTED+last {row[2]:9,}  sorted+rand {row[3]:8,}")

blocks.prompt: Randomizing the pivot changes the worst-case running time to what?
blocks.answer: Nothing: the worst case is still O(n²) (an unlucky random pick every time). What changes is that no particular input causes it, so the **expected** time on every input is Θ(n log n).

Θ(n²): every pivot is the max or min (Lomuto on sorted input)
